candidates.title: Empirical comparison of generate–verify–repair pipelines vs LLM-only and templated automation for NetOps change correctness
candidates.research_question: Does a generate–verify–repair pipeline (LLM generation + deterministic network verifier + automated repair loop) produce fewer unsafe network changes than (a) LLM-only generation and (b) traditional templated automation on a standardized NetOps change workload?
hypotheses: A generate–verify–repair pipeline yields a lower unsafe-change rate (fraction of proposed changes that violate reachability/policy) than an LLM-only pipeline.
Generate–verify–repair will reduce high-severity failures (policy-violations causing reachability loss) relative to templated automation for intent-driven, non-templateable changes.

The number of verifier-assisted repair iterations required per change will be small (median ≤2) and will produce materially lower unsafe-change rates even when the verifier has nonzero false-negative rate.
candidates.proposed_design: Construct a standardized workload of 500 NetOps intents sampled from public/synthesized topology/config templates (mix: 60% templateable changes, 40% complex intent-driven changes). Implement three pipelines: (A) LLM-only: prompt LLM to produce CLI/config change; (B) Generate–verify–repair: LLM generates change, deterministic verifier (Batfish-style) checks properties, on failure invoke LLM repair loop up to 3 iterations; (C) Templated automation: rule-based template generator for templateable subset and operator-specified fallback for complex intents. Use a deterministic network verifier as ground-truth oracle to label safety (reachability and policy constraints). Freeze prompts, seeds, and repair-loop stopping rules in a preregistration. Execute all pipelines for the same intent set; log all model calls, verifier outcomes, repair iterations, and wall-clock latencies.
candidates.expected_data: Per-intent records: proposed-change text, verifier label (pass/fail), severity of failure (reachability/policy), number of repair iterations, total model calls, wall-clock latency (ms), and final accepted-change status. Expect LLM-only to have highest unsafe-change rate, generate–verify–repair to substantially reduce unsafe changes particularly on complex intents, and templated automation to perform best on templateable subset but worse on complex intents.
candidates.primary_outcome: Unsafe-change rate (fraction of intents whose final accepted change fails verifier checks) difference between generate–verify–repair and each baseline.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute unsafe-change rates per pipeline with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals; perform pairwise proportion tests (chi-square or Fisher exact as appropriate) with Bonferroni correction. Subgroup analyses for templateable vs complex intents. Analyze repair-iteration counts distribution and correlate iterations with severity using logistic regression. Report latency and model-call overheads per saved unsafe change and present cost–benefit trade-offs.
risks: Synthesized workload may not capture production heterogeneity, limiting external validity.
Verifier limitations (modeling abstractions) could mislabel edge-case semantics, affecting measured unsafe-change rates.
Integration of verifier and repair loop may be sensitive to prompt formulation, making results prompt-dependent.

candidates.title: Adversarial robustness of LLM-driven NetOps pipelines and defense trade-offs
candidates.research_question: How effective are input-sanitization, instruction-filtering, verifier-gating, and combined defenses at reducing adversarial-success rates against LLM-driven NetOps pipelines, and what are their latency and false-positive trade-offs?
hypotheses: LLM-driven NetOps pipelines without defenses exhibit a substantial adversarial-success rate when presented with NetOps-formatted adversarial inputs.

A combined defense (sanitization + instruction-filtering + verifier-gating) reduces adversarial-success rate significantly more than any single defense but incurs higher latency and false-positive blocking on benign inputs.
Input-sanitization alone yields lower latency overhead but will have higher adversarial false-negatives (missed attacks) compared to verifier-gating approaches.
candidates.proposed_design: Curate an adversarial corpus of 600 NetOps-formatted attacks (adversarial intents, maliciously crafted CLI snippets, prompt-injection patterns) derived from public prompt-injection studies and NetOps-tailored perturbations. Build a baseline LLM pipeline that executes generated changes only after LLM output. Implement defenses: (D1) input-sanitization (token-level removal/escaping), (D2) instruction-filtering (reject inputs containing suspicious patterns), (D3) verifier-gating (invoke deterministic verifier before execution; block on failures), and (D4) combined (D1+D2+D3). For a control set, include 600 benign NetOps intents to measure false-positive blocking. For each defense variant and baseline, measure adversarial-success (attack leads to unsafe verifier pass or malicious action), verifier pass/fail, latency (ms), and defense false-positive rate on benign inputs. Freeze defense rules and thresholds in preregistration.
candidates.expected_data: Per-attempt labels: adversarial-success (yes/no), verifier pass/fail, latency (ms), defense decision (blocked/allowed), and number of tool/model calls. Expect high adversarial-success in baseline, substantial reduction with combined defense, and measurable latency increase; input-sanitization expected to show lowest latency but higher residual adversarial-success.
candidates.primary_outcome: Reduction in adversarial-success rate (fractional decrease relative to baseline) for each defense variant.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare adversarial-success rates across arms using proportion tests (chi-square) with multiple comparisons correction. Model latency–security trade-offs via Pareto analysis and logistic regression (adversarial-success ~ latency + defense type). Report defense false-positive rates on benign inputs and compute ROC for detection components. Provide qualitative attack examples that bypass each defense and root-cause analysis.
risks: Curated adversarial corpus may not capture future or unseen attack variants, limiting external validity.
Blocking/sanitization defenses may prevent legitimate operator intents, causing operational friction not fully captured in simulation.
Defense implementations could interact with specific LLM behaviors in a non-generalizable way across model versions.

candidates.title: Safety–latency trade-offs from verifier-invocation strategies: per-change, batched, and lazy verification in agentic NetOps
candidates.research_question: How do verifier-invocation strategies (per-change synchronous verification, batched verification, and lazy/asynchronous verification) affect verified-correct fraction, throughput, and operator-observed latency, and which batching parameters yield Pareto-optimal safety–latency trade-offs for realistic NetOps workloads?
hypotheses: Per-change (immediate) verification yields the highest verified-correct fraction but the lowest throughput and highest operator-observed latency.
Time-window or size-based batching recovers most of the safety of per-change verification while providing substantially higher throughput up to a workload-dependent batch threshold.
There exists a Pareto-optimal batching parameter (batch size or time window) that balances verified-correct fraction and mean latency for representative NetOps workloads.
candidates.proposed_design: Simulate a workload of N=1000 change requests sampled from a synthesized NetOps workload distribution (mix of small template changes and complex intent-driven changes). Implement three orchestration policies: (A) Per-change synchronous verification (invoke verifier for every change), (B) Time-window/size batching (accumulate for T seconds or up to B changes then run verifier), and (C) Lazy verification (allow immediate simulated execution, verify asynchronously and revert/alert on failures with rollback cost model). Sweep batching parameters T ∈ {0.5,1,2,5} seconds and B ∈ {5,10,20,50}. Use deterministic verifier as ground truth; simulate verifier latency and rollback costs; record verified-correct fraction, throughput (changes/sec), mean and percentile latencies, verifier CPU-time, and rollback frequency/costs. Freeze workload generator and seeds.
candidates.expected_data: Task-level records for 1000 changes per policy/parameterization: verified-correct fraction, throughput, mean and percentile latencies, verifier compute time, and rollback frequency/costs. Expect per-change verification to maximize safety but incur high latency and compute; batching to show diminishing safety loss up to a moderate batch threshold while gaining throughput; lazy verification to show highest throughput but nontrivial rollback costs.
candidates.primary_outcome: Pareto frontier of verified-correct fraction versus mean operator-observed latency; identification of batching (T,B) points on the frontier.
candidates.analysis_outline: For each policy/parameter, compute verified-correct fraction and latency; plot Pareto frontiers. Use regression to model verified-correct fraction as a function of batch size and workload mix; perform sensitivity analyses across workload mixes and verifier-latency distributions. Report compute cost per verified change and expected rollback cost for lazy verification with bootstrap confidence intervals.
risks: Simulated workload may not mirror production burstiness, affecting optimal batching estimates.
Verifier runtime variability in real deployments could change observed trade-offs.
Rollback simulations may under- or over-estimate real operational recovery costs and human intervention delays.

candidates.title: Limits of LLM self-correction for NetOps: efficacy comparison with verifier-assisted repair
candidates.research_question: Can LLMs reliably self-correct NetOps-specific errors (configuration mistakes or policy violations) without external deterministic verifier signals, and how does self-correction performance compare to verifier-assisted repair?
hypotheses: LLM-only self-correction (internal reasoning or chained retries without verifier signals) will achieve substantially lower final safety (verifier-pass rate) than verifier-assisted repair for NetOps errors.
Providing LLMs with structured failure examples or few-shot repair demonstrations improves self-correction success but does not attain verifier-assisted performance for complex intent-driven errors.
LLM confidence estimates or calibration scores are poorly predictive of actual verifier-pass outcomes when self-correcting without an external oracle.
candidates.proposed_design: Prepare a dataset of 400 synthetic NetOps failure cases (LLM-generated changes that intentionally fail deterministic verifier checks), spanning simple syntax errors, semantic misconfigurations, and policy violations. Define two interventions: (S1) LLM self-correction only—present the LLM the failing change and ask it to revise up to 3 times without access to the verifier verdict (but provide natural-language description of failure type in some arms); (S2) verifier-assisted repair—provide the verifier verdict and counterexamples and allow up to 3 repair iterations. Freeze prompts, few-shot exemplars, and seeds. After each iteration collect proposed change and evaluate with deterministic verifier to label pass/fail. Record model confidence estimates where available.
candidates.expected_data: Per-case records: initial failing change type, each revision text, verifier pass/fail after each revision, number of iterations to pass (if any), model-assigned confidence, total model calls, and latency. Expect verifier-assisted repair to achieve higher pass rates and fewer iterations; self-correction to succeed primarily on simple syntax/formatting failures.
candidates.primary_outcome: Final verifier-pass rate after up to 3 self-correction iterations (LLM-only) compared to verifier-assisted repair.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare final pass rates using proportion tests with confidence intervals. Stratify by failure type (syntax vs semantic vs policy). Assess iteration counts via survival analysis (time-to-pass in iterations). Evaluate predictive power of model confidence using ROC/AUC and calibration plots. Perform qualitative failure-mode analysis of cases where self-correction failed but verifier-assisted repair succeeded.
risks: LLM self-correction outcomes are highly prompt-sensitive, limiting reproducibility across prompt designs and model versions.
Dataset of failure cases may omit rare but operationally critical error modes.
Relying on model confidence requires support from the chosen LLM API and may not generalize across providers.
